title: Testing Equivalent Expressions with Desmos Sliders
description: Learn a fast, reliable way to answer "which expression is equivalent?" questions in two or more variables: give each variable a Desmos slider, pick random values, and let the numbers pick the matching answer choice.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep what you tried, even if you got stuck. You can continue without submitting an answer.

Let the values compare the long products

The opening expression needs several expansions, followed by a subtraction of an entire product. A slider gives a variable a value you can change, so Desmos can compare numerical results instead.

We’ll start with two simple letters to learn the controls, then return to the longer expression.

Read the numerical values

The calculator starts at \(a=2,b=3\). Read the value of the original and compare the choices. Then move the sliders and see which choice keeps matching.

content.prompt: At \(a=2,b=3\), the original \(a(2b+3)\) displays \(18\). Enter each choice with the same slider values. Which one matches?
content.explanation: B matches the original’s displayed value of \(18\). The sliders did the calculation; the other choices give different values at the same inputs.
content.hint: Keep the sliders at the same values for the original and every choice. Compare the displayed results.

blocks.html:
A mismatch rules out a choice

Equivalent expressions match at every allowed set of inputs. If a choice gives a different value once, eliminate it.

A single matching test can be a coincidence, so test another set when choices tie. Numerical tests help select among choices; they do not prove an identity.

content.prompt: At the same allowed slider values, the original displays 17 and one choice displays 18. What should you do?
choices: Keep that choice because it might match at another set of allowed values.
Change only that choice’s slider values until its display becomes 17.
Eliminate that choice; one mismatch rules it out.
Accept that choice because a difference of one is close enough for equivalence.
content.hint: A matching choice must agree with the original at the same allowed inputs.
content.solution: The original and this choice disagree at one legal input set. That rules the choice out. Continue comparing the other choices using the same values: C.
content.explanation: Good catch. One mismatch rules out a choice. Keep the same values for the remaining comparisons and retest any ties.

blocks.html:
Set, Compare, Retest

  1. Type the original and give each variable a slider.
  2. Use distinct ordinary values, such as 2 and 3.
  3. Test every choice with those same values.
  4. If choices tie, change the values and retest the survivors.

Choose values that separate the choices

At \(a=b=1\), \(2ab\) and \(a+b\) both equal 2. At \(a=2,b=3\), they differ. Zero, one, and repeated values can hide differences; use other allowed values when they do.

content.prompt: You test the choices using \(a=1\) and \(b=1\). Two different choices both equal the original. What should you do?
choices: Pick whichever of the two matched expressions looks simpler — both must be equivalent
Conclude that none of the four expressions is actually equivalent to the original
Re-test with other values like \(a=2, b=3\), since \(0\) and \(1\) often make different expressions match
Set both variables to \(0\) instead and see whether the same two choices still match
content.explanation: A tie at \(1\) (or \(0\)) usually means the test values were too friendly. Switch to different, non-trivial numbers and the imposter will break away from the original.

blocks.html:
Compare another original

At \(a=2,b=3\), read \(a(3a+2b)-2b(a-b)\). Compare its output with each candidate row, then change the sliders to test the surviving match again.

content.hint: Use the two slider values shown. Compare each candidate’s number with the original, then retest any tie.
content.prompt: Try one yourself. The original is \(2p(3p-q)+q(4p+q)\). Use the calculator with \(p=2, q=3\) (original value \(=45\)). Which choice is equivalent?
content.explanation: A displays \(45\), matching the original at \(p=2,q=3\). The other choices display different numbers. Compare another allowed value set if any choices tie.

calculator.title: Test each choice at p = 2, q = 3

blocks.html:
For x and y, use uppercase

Lowercase x and y have graphing jobs in Desmos. Replace every x with X and every y with Y, in the original and all choices. Uppercase X and Y can have sliders, so the comparison works the same way.

content.prompt: The question uses variables \(x\) and \(y\), but Desmos won't create sliders for them. What's the fix?
choices: Replace \(x\) and \(y\) with capital \(X\) and \(Y\) everywhere, then add sliders
Give up on using sliders, since the method cannot handle questions written with \(x\) and \(y\)
Set \(x=0\) and \(y=0\), compare the values once, and keep whichever choice matches
Create one shared slider and use its value for both \(x\) and \(y\) in every choice
content.explanation: Capital \(X\) and \(Y\) act like normal variables in Desmos, so they get sliders. Swap them in the original and in every choice, then test as usual.

blocks.html:
Return to the longer products

Try the opening question again. Choose your test values and compare every choice with the original.

content.hint: Use X and Y in place of x and y throughout. Give them distinct values, keep the full subtracted product grouped, and compare all four choices. Retest any tie.
content.solution:
Enter sliders \(X=2,\ Y=3\).
Enter \((2X-Y)(X+3Y)^2-(X+Y)(X-2Y)^2\). Desmos displays \(41\).
Enter all four choices using those same capital letters. They display \(41,-31,257,201\).
Only A matches. At \(X=3,Y=2\), the original and A both display \(319\).
content.explanation: A matches. The sliders separated the choices without expanding and collecting the cubic terms.

content.prompt: How do you compare expressions fairly with sliders, and what do you do if choices tie?
choices: Give each expression sliders set to zeros, and keep the first choice that matches.
Give each expression its own values, then compare its result with the original.
Give every variable a slider, compare expressions at the same allowed values, and retest ties.
Give one variable a slider, leave the others undefined, and compare the expressions.
content.explanation: Each comparison uses one complete value set. If choices tie, change to another allowed set and retest them.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.title: Build your own slider comparison
content.instructions_html:
Start with an empty calculator. Replace every x and y in the original and choices with uppercase X and Y.

  1. Create sliders X and Y and choose distinct values other than 0 or 1.
  2. Enter the original and all four choices on five separate rows.
  3. Compare their displayed values. If choices tie, change the sliders and retest.

Decide which choice keeps matching before continuing. Record your answer on the next card; use Previous to return to this comparison if needed.

feedback.success_message_html: Your comparison entries are ready. Compare the values, retest any ties, and choose the match on the next card.
feedback.retry_message_html: Keep the same two uppercase variables in all five expressions. Include both slider definitions and compare every choice.

targeted_hints.message_html: Define X and Y on their own rows so both can act as sliders.
Choose distinct values other than 0 or 1, then compare all five results.
Use uppercase X and Y everywhere; lowercase x and y have graphing roles.
You need two slider definitions, the original, and four choices: seven math rows.

feedback.solution_html:
One setup is \(X=2\), \(Y=3\), then these five rows:

\[\begin{aligned}&(X+2Y)^2(X-Y)\\&{}-(X-2Y)^2(X+Y)\end{aligned}\]

  • \(6XY^2-8X^3\)
  • \(6X^2Y-8Y^3\)
  • \(6X^2Y-4Y^3\)
  • \(2X^3\)

Read and compare their values. Change the sliders to test again.

shared_prompt.title: Record your comparison
shared_prompt.html:
Which expression is equivalent to

\[\begin{aligned}&(x+2y)^2(x-y)\\&{}-(x-2y)^2(x+y)\end{aligned}\text{?}\]

Use Previous if you need to revisit your calculator comparison.

content.explanation: At \(X=2,Y=3\), the original displays −144. A, B, C, and D display 44, −144, −36, and 16, so B is the only survivor. At \(X=3,Y=2\), B still matches the original at 44. At \(X=Y=1\), A and B tie at −2, so that test alone would not separate them.

content.html:
Compare at the same values

Eliminate mismatches and retest any tied choices.
